targetQuery: HTTP methods, status codes, caching, cookies explained (with idempotency and HTTP/1.1 vs 2 vs 3)
comparedAgainst: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Methods — fetched. MDN's methods page is a descriptive reference table (safe/idempotent/cacheable columns) with links out to per-method pages; no running server, no wire bytes, no 100-continue demonstration, no worked idempotency proof. This article's five TcpListener programs (framing, idempotency with real stored-state divergence, status families with a real Expect/100-Continue round trip, ETag caching with a real 200->304->200 cycle, cookie wire mechanics) are a materially deeper and more concrete treatment of the same ground.

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Caching — fetched. MDN's caching guide explains ETag/304 conceptually with illustrative (non-executable) header snippets and mentions hashing as one option among many with no algorithm specifics; it never runs anything. This article's caching program computes a real SHA-256 ETag, gets a genuine 304 on an unmodified resource, and then gets a genuine fresh 200 with a new tag after the content actually changes underneath a stale conditional request — a real trace MDN's page does not attempt.

RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics), RFC 9111 (HTTP Caching), RFC 9112 (HTTP/1.1), RFC 9113 (HTTP/2), RFC 9114 (HTTP/3), RFC 9000 (QUIC), RFC 6265 (Cookies), RFC 5789 (PATCH) — all eight fetched directly (plaintext editions) and checked section-by-section against the article's specific claims and quotations; see justification.
Microsoft Learn: TcpListener.AcceptTcpClientAsync and TcpListener.Start method pages — both fetched; see the citation-accuracy finding below.
justification:
Ran `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/networking/http-explained.md` seven times independently in this session (two invocations launched in parallel, then five more sequentially) from PowerShell. Every run reported `PASS networking/http-explained.md  blocks=13 executed=6` with no flakiness, matching the writer's claim exactly; the server/client synchronization in all five programs (loopback TcpListener bound to port 0, client connects after Start(), AcceptTcpClientAsync/Handle loops matched to the exact number of client connections each program makes) held up under repeated runs including two concurrent processes competing for CPU. I re-traced the idempotency, Expect/100-Continue, caching and cookie programs by hand against their printed output and they are internally consistent (see below).

Idempotency table and definitions (item 2 of the brief): verified word-for-word against RFC 9110's own summary table in section 9.2 ('| Method | Safe | Idempotent | Section |' listing CONNECT no/no, DELETE no/yes, GET yes/yes, HEAD yes/yes, OPTIONS yes/yes, POST no/no, PUT no/yes, TRACE yes/yes) — the article's table matches this exactly. Section 9.2.2's actual text is 'A request method is considered "idempotent" if the intended effect on the server of multiple identical requests with that method is the same as the effect for a single such request. Of the request methods defined by this specification, PUT, DELETE, and safe request methods are idempotent' — the article's paraphrase is precise, not folklore. RFC 5789 section 2 reads verbatim 'PATCH is neither safe nor idempotent as defined by [RFC2616], Section 9.1,' matching the article's citation exactly. This is the most precise treatment of this claim I have seen outside the RFC itself — most tutorials just assert the table without the safe-methods and PATCH nuance the article gets right.

Expect/100-Continue demo (item 3): the mechanism is real, not a simplification. RFC 9110 section 10.1.1 requires that 'A client that will wait for a 100 (Continue) response before sending the request content MUST send an Expect header field containing a 100-continue expectation' and that 'A server that sends a 100 (Continue) response MUST ultimately send a final status code, once it receives and processes the request content.' The article's client does exactly this (writes headers+Expect, blocks on ReadHead for the interim response, only then writes the body), and the server's ReadHead/ReadBody split is the correct fix for the deadlock the article names: had the server used the unified ReadMessage helper (used everywhere else), it would call the body-reading loop immediately after the blank line, blocking on net.ReadAsync for Content-Length bytes the client is deliberately withholding until it sees the interim response the server hasn't sent yet -- a genuine mutual wait, not a strawman. I traced this by hand against the code and it is correct. Section 15.2.1 confirms 'The server intends to send a final response after the request has been fully received and acted upon,' backing the article's 'exactly one more response' framing.

Caching/ETag demo (item 4): traced the three-request sequence by hand. `Handle` recomputes `Etag(report)` from the closed-over `report` variable on every call, so the 2nd request's `If-None-Match` (the value the 1st response handed out) compares equal while `report` is unchanged, yielding a genuine `304` with zero body bytes; after `report` is reassigned, the 3rd request resends the now-stale first ETag, the freshly computed hash differs, and the server correctly falls through to a full `200` with a new tag. This is a real 200->304->200-after-change round trip, not staged output. RFC 9110 section 8.8.1 explicitly endorses this exact construction ('A collision-resistant hash function applied to the representation data is also sufficient' for a strong validator), so the technique is textbook-correct, not merely defensible.

Cookie wire mechanics (item 5): verified against RFC 6265 section 4.2.1's grammar (`cookie-string = cookie-pair *( ";" SP cookie-pair )`) and its own commentary ('Notice that the cookie attributes are not returned... whether the cookie was set with the Secure or HttpOnly attributes'). The demo's `jar = login.Cookie!.Split(';')[0]` strips Path/HttpOnly before resending, exactly matching the grammar, and the article's prose and the 'find the bug' exercise both correctly locate the failure mode (sending raw attributes back as if they were cookie-pairs). Accurate.

HTTP/1.1 vs 2 vs 3 (item 6): fetched RFC 9113 section 5 ('Streams are largely independent of each other, so a blocked or stalled request or response does not prevent progress on other streams') and RFC 9114 sections 1.1-1.2 ('a lost or reordered packet causes all active transactions to experience a stall regardless of whether that transaction was directly impacted' for HTTP/2-over-TCP, and 'By providing reliability at the stream level... QUIC has the capability to improve the performance of HTTP' for HTTP/3). The article's claims -- HTTP/2 fixes application-layer HOL blocking via multiplexing but inherits TCP's transport-layer HOL blocking, HTTP/3 fixes that by replacing the transport with QUIC -- match this exactly and are not oversimplified; the exercise correctly distinguishes 'zero queuing at the HTTP layer' (already true at HTTP/2) from 'a lost packet only stalls its own stream' (the actual HTTP/3 improvement), which is a real and commonly-blurred distinction most treatments get sloppy about.

TcpListener.Start() claim (item 7): substantively true -- Microsoft Learn's TcpListener.Start page (fetched) states 'If a connection request is received, the Start method will queue the request and continue listening for additional requests' and that AcceptTcpClient/AcceptSocket 'remove a connection from the incoming connection queue,' which is exactly the 'listens immediately, connections queue until Accept is called' behavior the article describes. But the article's inline citation for this sentence links to the AcceptTcpClientAsync page, which (fetched in full) says nothing about Start(), backlog queuing, or when the socket enters LISTEN state -- it only documents the async accept call itself. The claim is right; the citation is attached to the wrong page. This is exactly the citation-accuracy failure mode EDITORIAL_BRIEF calls out ('a citation attached to a sentence its page does not support is a finding').

Genuine differentiation vs. published sources (item 8): both fetched MDN pages (Methods, Caching) are descriptive/illustrative only -- categorization tables and non-executable header snippets, no server code, no wire captures, no 100-continue trace, no real hash-based ETag round trip. This article's 'a real TcpListener server, not just described' framing is honestly earned, not marketing.

One factual error found (item 9), which caps the score: the sentence introducing ETag -- '`ETag` supplies a validator: an opaque token the server can recompute later and compare, defined once in RFC 9110 as identifying "one or more stored responses" ([section 8.8.3])' -- puts a direct quotation in quote marks and cites RFC 9110 section 8.8.3 for it. I fetched and read RFC 9110 section 8.8.3 and its subsections (8.8.3.1-8.8.3.3) in full; that text defines ETag as 'an opaque validator for differentiating between multiple representations of the same resource' and never contains the words 'one or more stored responses.' That exact phrase -- 'One or more entity tags, indicating one or more stored responses, can be used in an If-None-Match header field for response validation' -- is in RFC 9111 (Caching), not RFC 9110, in the section describing how a cache builds a validation request. The article separately cites RFC 9111 elsewhere in the same paragraph for the freshness/validation split, so the source material was clearly read, but this specific quoted clause is misattributed to a section of a different RFC that does not contain it. A quotation marked as verbatim and pinned to a specific section that does not say it is a demonstrable factual error, not a paraphrase-precision nit, and the brief's 'never fabricate' rule and the gauntlet rubric ('a single factual error caps the technical score at 7') both apply directly.

Two further citation-precision issues, each minor on its own but adding up alongside the misattribution above: 'Safe methods... are idempotent by construction (RFC 9110, section 9.2.1)' cites 9.2.1 (which only defines 'safe' and never states the safe-implies-idempotent relationship), when the actual sentence 'PUT, DELETE, and safe request methods are idempotent' is in section 9.2.2. And the HTTP/1.1 head-of-line-blocking table cell cites RFC 9112 section 9.3 broadly ('Persistence'), while the specific supporting requirement ('a server... MUST send the corresponding responses in the same order that the requests were received') is in the nested subsection 9.3.2 ('Pipelining'). Everything else checked out; the technical depth, correctness of the runnable code, and honesty of the version-comparison table are genuinely strong and above the bar the comparison sources set. Withholding one point beyond the mandatory cap for the two additional citation-precision issues stacked on top of the misattributed quote.

issues.location: "Telling a client its copy is still good" section, the sentence introducing ETag: '`ETag` supplies a validator: an opaque token the server can recompute later and compare, defined once in RFC 9110 as identifying "one or more stored responses" ([section 8.8.3]).'
issues.problem: The quoted phrase "one or more stored responses" does not appear in RFC 9110 section 8.8.3 (fetched and read in full: it defines an entity tag as 'an opaque validator for differentiating between multiple representations of the same resource,' nothing about 'stored responses'). That exact phrase is in RFC 9111 (Caching) instead, in the sentence 'One or more entity tags, indicating one or more stored responses, can be used in an If-None-Match header field for response validation.' A direct quotation pinned to a specific section of the wrong RFC is a fabricated/misattributed citation, which the brief's 'never fabricate' rule and 'cite where the claim is made, and make sure that page supports that clause' rule both flag directly.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either drop the quotation marks and just paraphrase RFC 9110 8.8.3's actual definition ('an opaque validator for differentiating between multiple representations of the same resource'), or keep the quoted phrase and re-cite it to RFC 9111 (the correct source), not RFC 9110 section 8.8.3.

issues.location: "A message is a start line, headers, a blank line, an optional body" section, the sentence about `TcpListener.Start` and connection queuing, cited to the Microsoft Learn AcceptTcpClientAsync page.
issues.problem: The underlying claim (Start() puts the socket into a listening state immediately and connections queue in a backlog before Accept is called) is true -- confirmed on Microsoft Learn's TcpListener.Start page ('If a connection request is received, the Start method will queue the request and continue listening... To remove a connection from the incoming connection queue, use either the AcceptTcpClient method or the AcceptSocket method') -- but the article's inline citation and its front-matter source entry both point at the AcceptTcpClientAsync page instead, which (fetched in full) says nothing about Start(), the backlog, or LISTEN state; it only documents the async accept call's own behavior.
issues.fixLooksLike: Cite (and add to front-matter sources) the TcpListener.Start method page (learn.microsoft.com/.../system.net.sockets.tcplistener.start), which is the page that actually supports this sentence.

issues.location: "Methods, and which ones are safe to repeat" section: 'Safe methods... are idempotent by construction ([RFC 9110, section 9.2.1]).'
issues.problem: Section 9.2.1 only defines what 'safe' means and does not itself state that safe methods are idempotent. The explicit sentence 'Of the request methods defined by this specification, PUT, DELETE, and safe request methods are idempotent' is in section 9.2.2, the section the article cites two sentences earlier for the idempotent definition itself.
issues.fixLooksLike: Cite 9.2.2 (or both 9.2.1 and 9.2.2) for the safe-implies-idempotent claim instead of 9.2.1 alone.

issues.location: HTTP/1.1 vs 2 vs 3 table, HTTP/1.1 row, 'Where head-of-line blocking is left' column, cited to RFC 9112 section 9.3.
issues.problem: Section 9.3 ('Persistence') is a general introduction to keep-alive connections; the specific requirement backing the claim -- a server 'MUST send the corresponding responses in the same order that the requests were received' -- is in the nested subsection 9.3.2 ('Pipelining'), not stated in 9.3's own text.
issues.fixLooksLike: Cite section 9.3.2 specifically rather than the parent section 9.3.

issues.problem: Truncating a SHA-256 digest to 8 hex characters (32 bits) is fine for this demo's two distinct contents, and RFC 9110 8.8.1 explicitly endorses 'a collision-resistant hash function applied to the representation data' as a strong-validator basis -- but the article calls the truncated 8-char tag itself 'a strong validator' with no caveat that truncating a collision-resistant hash this far materially weakens the collision resistance the strong-validator property leans on (32 bits collides at roughly 2^16 distinct values by the birthday bound, versus practically-never for the full 256-bit digest).
issues.fixLooksLike: A one-clause caveat, e.g. 'truncated here for a short reader-facing tag; a real implementation would send the full digest,' so the strong-validator claim isn't read as endorsing 8-hex-char ETags in production.
